claim: The dataset was created by linking information from the California Cancer Registry (CCR) and California Birth Statistical Master File.
source: The dataset was created by linking information from the California Cancer Registry (CCR) and California Birth Statistical Master File, allowing the capture of siblings and parents of cancer probands, along with their cancer incidence (California Cancer Registry, 2018).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the data sources used to create the dataset, with a citation to the California Cancer Registry.

claim: The linked dataset comprehensively encompassed all cancer cases 0–26 years old, as well as their sibling and mother cancers, diagnosed from 1989 to 2015 in California.
source: The linked dataset comprehensively encompassed all cancer cases 0–26 years old, as well as their sibling and mother cancers, diagnosed from 1989 to 2015 in California.
evidence: Direct statement about the scope and time period of the dataset.

claim: The dataset included a total of 121,571 individuals.
source: Overall, the dataset included a total of 121,571 individuals.
evidence: Explicit numerical data about the total dataset size.

claim: From 1989 to 2015, 29,631 cancer patients and 62,863 healthy family members were identified.
source: From 1989 to 2015, we identified 29,631 cancer patients and 62,863 healthy family members.
evidence: Explicit numerical data from the study population presented in the abstract.

claim: From 1989 to 2015, a total of 29,249 pediatric and AYA patients with a primary malignancy were identified.
source: From 1989 to 2015, we identified a total of 29,249 pediatric and AYA patients with a primary malignancy, comprising 29,072 probands, 112 affected siblings (from 110 families), and 65 affected mothers.
evidence: Explicit numerical data about the study population breakdown.

claim: 112 affected siblings from 110 families were identified.
source: From 1989 to 2015, we identified a total of 29,249 pediatric and AYA patients with a primary malignancy, comprising 29,072 probands, 112 affected siblings (from 110 families), and 65 affected mothers.
evidence: Explicit numerical data about affected siblings.

claim: 65 affected mothers were identified.
source: From 1989 to 2015, we identified a total of 29,249 pediatric and AYA patients with a primary malignancy, comprising 29,072 probands, 112 affected siblings (from 110 families), and 65 affected mothers.
evidence: Explicit numerical data about affected mothers.

claim: All siblings were diagnosed after the proband's diagnosis.
source: All siblings were diagnosed after the proband's diagnosis as defined, and 56 (86%) of the 65 mothers were diagnosed after the proband's diagnosis.
evidence: Direct statement about the temporal relationship of sibling diagnoses.

claim: 56 (86%) of the 65 mothers were diagnosed after the proband's diagnosis.
source: All siblings were diagnosed after the proband's diagnosis as defined, and 56 (86%) of the 65 mothers were diagnosed after the proband's diagnosis.
evidence: Explicit numerical data with percentage calculation.

claim: 387 SPMs were identified among all pediatric and AYA probands.
source: We also identified 387 SPMs among all pediatric and AYA probands (Table 2).
evidence: Explicit numerical data about second primary malignancies.

claim: There was a 3.32-fold increased relative risk of any cancer among siblings and mothers who have a proband with cancer in the same family (95% CI: 2.85–3.85).
source: Overall, we found a 3.32-fold (95% CI: 2.85–3.85) increased relative risk of any cancer among siblings and mothers who have a proband with cancer in the same family.
evidence: Explicit statistical result with confidence interval from the study analysis.

claim: There was a 2.97-fold increased relative risk of any cancer given a proband with hematologic cancers (95% CI: 2.30–3.78).
source: Briefly, we found a 2.97-fold (95% CI: 2.30–3.78) increased relative risk of any cancer given a proband with hematologic cancers and a 4.54-fold (95% CI: 3.82–5.35) increased relative risk of any cancer given a proband with solid cancers.
evidence: Explicit statistical result with confidence interval.

claim: There was a 4.54-fold increased relative risk of any cancer given a proband with solid cancers (95% CI: 3.82–5.35).
source: Briefly, we found a 2.97-fold (95% CI: 2.30–3.78) increased relative risk of any cancer given a proband with hematologic cancers and a 4.54-fold (95% CI: 3.82–5.35) increased relative risk of any cancer given a proband with solid cancers.
evidence: Explicit statistical result with confidence interval.

claim: Higher relative risks among siblings and mothers were observed given probands with leukemias, lymphomas, CNS tumors, retinoblastomas, renal tumors, sarcomas, germ cell tumors (GCTs), epithelial neoplasms, and other unspecified neoplasms.
source: When stratified by cancer type, higher relative risks among siblings and mothers were observed given probands with leukemias, lymphomas, CNS tumors, retinoblastomas, renal tumors, sarcomas, germ cell tumors (GCTs), epithelial neoplasms, and other unspecified neoplasms (Figure 1A).
evidence: Explicit statement supported by Figure 1A showing the data.

claim: There was a 2.68-fold increased risk of hematologic cancers among siblings and mothers of a proband with hematologic cancer (95% CI: 1.68–4.06).
source: For the relative risk of specific cancer types, we found a 2.68-fold (95% CI: 1.68–4.06) increased risk of hematologic cancers among siblings and mothers of a proband with hematologic cancer, and a 6.78-fold (95% CI: 5.58–8.16) increased relative risk of solid cancers among siblings and mothers of a proband with solid cancer (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Explicit statistical result with confidence interval.

claim: There was a 6.78-fold increased relative risk of solid cancers among siblings and mothers of a proband with solid cancer (95% CI: 5.58–8.16).
source: For the relative risk of specific cancer types, we found a 2.68-fold (95% CI: 1.68–4.06) increased risk of hematologic cancers among siblings and mothers of a proband with hematologic cancer, and a 6.78-fold (95% CI: 5.58–8.16) increased relative risk of solid cancers among siblings and mothers of a proband with solid cancer (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Explicit statistical result with confidence interval.

claim: Leukemias, lymphomas, CNS tumors, retinoblastoma, sarcomas, GCT, and epithelial neoplasms exhibited statistically significantly increased relative risk for the same type of cancer as the proband.
source: Furthermore, leukemias, lymphomas, CNS tumors, retinoblastoma, sarcomas, GCT, and epithelial neoplasms exhibited statistically significantly increased relative risk for the same type of cancer as the proband (Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Explicit statement supported by Figure 2 and supplementary data.

claim: Both Latinos (SIR = 4.98; 95% CI: 3.82–6.39) and non-Latino Blacks (SIR = 7.35; 95% CI: 3.36–13.95) exhibited significantly higher relative risk of any cancer in siblings and mothers when compared to non-Latino White subjects (SIR = 3.02; 95% CI: 2.12–4.16) given a proband with solid cancer.
source: Given a proband with solid cancer, both Latinos (SIR = 4.98; 95% CI: 3.82–6.39) and non-Latino Blacks (SIR = 7.35; 95% CI: 3.36–13.95) exhibited significantly higher relative risk of any cancer in siblings and mothers when compared to non-Latino White subjects (SIR = 3.02; 95% CI: 2.12–4.16).
evidence: Explicit statistical comparison across ethnic groups with confidence intervals.

claim: For hematologic cancers, higher familial risk was evident for Asian/Pacific Islanders (SIR = 7.56; 95% CI: 3.26–14.90) compared to non-Latino whites (SIR = 2.69; 95% CI: 1.62–4.20).
source: For hematologic cancers, higher familial risk was evident for Asian/Pacific Islanders (SIR = 7.56; 95% CI: 3.26–14.90) compared to non-Latino whites (SIR = 2.69; 95% CI: 1.62–4.20).
evidence: Explicit statistical comparison between ethnic groups with confidence intervals.

claim: The relative risk of any cancer for siblings and mothers given a proband with solid cancer was significantly higher among Latino subjects than NLW subjects (Latino: SIR = 4.98; 95% CI: 3.82–6.39; NLW: SIR = 3.02; 95% CI: 2.12–4.16; p=0.019).
source: When stratified by race/ethnicity, the relative risk of any cancer for siblings and mothers given a proband with solid cancer was significantly higher among Latino and non-Latino black subjects than NLW subjects (Latino: SIR = 4.98; 95% CI: 3.82–6.39; NLW: SIR = 3.02; 95% CI: 2.12–4.16; p=0.019) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Explicit statistical comparison with p-value and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Non-Latino Asians/Pacific Islanders had higher SIRs than NLW given a proband with hematologic cancer (SIR = 7.56; 95% CI: 3.26–14.90, p=0.023 compared to NLW).
source: Non-Latino Asians/Pacific Islanders (API) had higher SIRs than NLW given a proband with hematologic cancer (SIR = 7.56; 95% CI: 3.26–14.90, p=0.023 compared to NLW), and non-Latino Blacks had higher SIRs than NLW given a proband with any cancer (SIR = 6.96; 95% CI: 3.71–11.91, p=0.002 compared to NLW) or solid cancer (SIR = 7.35; 95% CI: 3.36–13.95, p=0.026 compares to NLW) (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: Explicit statistical comparison with p-value.

claim: Non-Latino Blacks had higher SIRs than NLW given a proband with any cancer (SIR = 6.96; 95% CI: 3.71–11.91, p=0.002 compared to NLW).
source: Non-Latino Asians/Pacific Islanders (API) had higher SIRs than NLW given a proband with hematologic cancer (SIR = 7.56; 95% CI: 3.26–14.90, p=0.023 compared to NLW), and non-Latino Blacks had higher SIRs than NLW given a proband with any cancer (SIR = 6.96; 95% CI: 3.71–11.91, p=0.002 compared to NLW) or solid cancer (SIR = 7.35; 95% CI: 3.36–13.95, p=0.026 compares to NLW) (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: Explicit statistical comparison with p-value.

claim: Non-Latino Blacks had higher SIRs than NLW given a proband with solid cancer (SIR = 7.35; 95% CI: 3.36–13.95, p=0.026 compared to NLW).
source: Non-Latino Asians/Pacific Islanders (API) had higher SIRs than NLW given a proband with hematologic cancer (SIR = 7.56; 95% CI: 3.26–14.90, p=0.023 compared to NLW), and non-Latino Blacks had higher SIRs than NLW given a proband with any cancer (SIR = 6.96; 95% CI: 3.71–11.91, p=0.002 compared to NLW) or solid cancer (SIR = 7.35; 95% CI: 3.36–13.95, p=0.026 compares to NLW) (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: Explicit statistical comparison with p-value.

claim: Latino subjects showed higher relative risk of solid cancers than NLW subjects (Latino: SIR = 7.94; 95% CI: 5.89–10.47; NLW: SIR = 4.41; 95% CI: 2.99–6.25; p=0.012).
source: For the relative risk of the same category of cancers given a proband with that type of cancer, Latino subjects also showed higher relative risk of solid cancers than NLW subjects (Latino: SIR = 7.94; 95% CI: 5.89–10.47; NLW: SIR = 4.41; 95% CI: 2.99–6.25; p=0.012) (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Explicit statistical comparison with p-value.

claim: SPMs among all childhood patients were enriched in families that exhibited familial risks.
source: Overall, SPMs among all childhood patients were enriched in families that exhibited familial risks; that is, those families with two or more primary cancer patients.
evidence: Direct statement about the enrichment pattern.

claim: 14 SPMs of 2432 members (0.58%) were found in families that exhibited familial risks (two or more primary cancers).
source: We found 14 SPMs of 2432 members (0.58%) in the families that exhibited familial risks (two or more primary cancers) and 373 SPMs of 119,136 members (0.31%) in families that did not exhibit familial risk (p=0.023) (Supplementary file 1E).
evidence: Explicit numerical data with percentage and statistical significance.

claim: 373 SPMs of 119,136 members (0.31%) were found in families that did not exhibit familial risk.
source: We found 14 SPMs of 2432 members (0.58%) in the families that exhibited familial risks (two or more primary cancers) and 373 SPMs of 119,136 members (0.31%) in families that did not exhibit familial risk (p=0.023) (Supplementary file 1E).
evidence: Explicit numerical data with percentage.

claim: The difference in SPM rates between families with and without familial risk was statistically significant (p=0.023).
source: We found 14 SPMs of 2432 members (0.58%) in the families that exhibited familial risks (two or more primary cancers) and 373 SPMs of 119,136 members (0.31%) in families that did not exhibit familial risk (p=0.023) (Supplementary file 1E).
evidence: Explicit p-value indicating statistical significance.

claim: There was a 7.27-fold increased risk of SPMs relative to the general population among children/AYAs with a FPM (SIR = 7.27; 95% CI: 6.56–8.03).
source: For relative risks, we found a 7.27-fold increased risk of SPMs relative to the general population among children/AYAs with a FPM (SIR = 7.27; 95% CI: 6.56–8.03).
evidence: Explicit statistical result with confidence interval.

claim: Most primary cancer types were associated with an elevated relative risk of SPMs.
source: Most primary cancer types were associated with an elevated relative risk of SPMs (Figure 3A).
evidence: Explicit statement supported by Figure 3A.

claim: A similar relative risk of all SPMs given a proband with cancer was observed among Latino subjects and NLW subjects (Latino: SIR = 6.85; 95% CI: 5.83–8.00; NLW: SIR = 6.65; 95% CI: 5.55–7.91; p=0.869).
source: When stratified by race/ethnicity, a similar relative risk of all SPMs given a proband with cancer was observed among Latino subjects and NLW subjects (Latino: SIR = 6.85; 95% CI: 5.83–8.00; NLW: SIR = 6.65; 95% CI: 5.55–7.91; p=0.869) (Figure 3B).
evidence: Explicit statistical comparison with p-value.

claim: The relative risk of all SPMs given a proband with any cancer was higher among non-Latino API subjects compared to NLW subjects (non-Latino API: SIR = 15.41; 95% CI: 10.85–21.24; p<0.001).
source: The relative risk of all SPMs given a proband with any cancer and solid cancers were higher among non-Latino API subjects compared to NLW subjects (any cancer, non-Latino API: SIR = 15.41; 95% CI: 10.85–21.24; p<0.001; hematologic cancers, non-Latino API: SIR = 18.90; 95% CI: 11.55–29.20; p<0.001) (Figure 3B).
evidence: Explicit statistical comparison with p-value.

claim: The relative risk of SPMs for hematologic cancers was higher among non-Latino API subjects compared to NLW subjects (non-Latino API: SIR = 18.90; 95% CI: 11.55–29.20; p<0.001).
source: The relative risk of all SPMs given a proband with any cancer and solid cancers were higher among non-Latino API subjects compared to NLW subjects (any cancer, non-Latino API: SIR = 15.41; 95% CI: 10.85–21.24; p<0.001; hematologic cancers, non-Latino API: SIR = 18.90; 95% CI: 11.55–29.20; p<0.001) (Figure 3B).
evidence: Explicit statistical comparison with p-value.

claim: The absolute risk of early-onset cancer is higher among young siblings and mothers in the current study (0.074%) compared to general population (0.023%) of the same age group.
source: Due to the rarity of childhood cancers, the absolute risk of early-onset cancer is very small, but still higher among young siblings and mothers in the current study (0.074%) compared to general population (0.023%, calculated from SEER) of the same age group.
evidence: Explicit comparison of absolute risk percentages with reference to SEER data.

claim: Li–Fraumeni syndrome caused by mutations in the tumor suppressor gene TP53 is associated with an increased risk of a spectrum of cancers diagnosed at early ages.
source: As an example of the former, Li–Fraumeni syndrome caused by mutations in the tumor suppressor gene TP53 is associated with an increased risk of a spectrum of cancers diagnosed at early ages (Saletta et al., 2015).
evidence: Explicit statement with citation to support the claim.

claim: IKZF1 and ARID5B genes are examples of low penetrance common genetic variations associated with pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) risk.
source: An example of low penetrance common genetic variations associated with cancer risk includes IKZF1 and ARID5B genes in pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) (Moriyama et al., 2015).
evidence: Explicit statement with citation to support the claim.

claim: Both high penetrance and low penetrance genetic variants may vary in frequency by race/ethnic group and cluster by families.
source: Both of these classes of variants may vary in frequency by race/ethnic group and cluster by families (Caswell-Jin et al., 2018; Walsh et al., 2013; Ricker et al., 2016).
evidence: Explicit statement with multiple citations to support the claim.

claim: Cancer incidence rates differ by race/ethnicity for many pediatric cancer types, such as leukemia and brain cancer.
source: Examination of cancer predisposition requires investigation in ethnic strata particularly where cancer incidence rates are known to differ as they do for many pediatric cancer types, such as leukemia (Feng and de Smith, 2020) and brain cancer (Ostrom et al., 2019).
evidence: Explicit statement with citations to support the claim.

claim: Among childhood cancer survivors, more second primary malignancy (SPM) cases are observed among non-Latino Whites (NLW) than Latino subjects.
source: Among childhood cancer survivors, more second primary malignancy (SPM) cases are observed among non-Latino Whites (NLW) than Latino subjects (Brown et al., 2019).
evidence: Explicit statement with citation to support the claim.

claim: Latino breast cancer survivors had lower risk of second cancers than NLW and NL Black women.
source: This is also reflected in adult cancers, where Latino breast cancer survivors had lower risk of second cancers than NLW and NL Black women (Calip et al., 2015).
evidence: Explicit statement with citation to support the claim.

claim: Germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants in cancer predisposition genes are found in approximately 10% of pediatric cancer patients.
source: Germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants in cancer predisposition genes are found in approximately 10% of pediatric cancer patients (Saletta et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015; Plon and Lupo, 2019; Ripperger et al., 2017), and may be inherited or arise de novo.
evidence: Explicit statement with multiple citations to support the claim.

claim: Germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants in cancer predisposition genes may be inherited or arise de novo.
source: Germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants in cancer predisposition genes are found in approximately 10% of pediatric cancer patients (Saletta et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015; Plon and Lupo, 2019; Ripperger et al., 2017), and may be inherited or arise de novo.
evidence: Explicit statement about the origin of germline variants.

claim: Highly penetrant inherited variants will contribute to clustering of cancer cases within the family.
source: Highly penetrant inherited variants will contribute to clustering of cancer cases within the family.
evidence: Direct statement about the relationship between highly penetrant variants and familial clustering.

claim: Shared environments within the family unit may be considered alongside genetic risk as potential causes for family-based cancer concordance.
source: Shared environments within the family unit may also be considered alongside genetic risk as potential causes for family-based cancer concordance.
evidence: Direct statement about environmental factors as potential contributors.

claim: The Swedish Family-Cancer Database has been used to assess familial concordance of a wide variety of cancers, leading to a deep understanding of familial relative risks.
source: Familial concordance of a wide variety of cancers has been assessed using the Swedish Family-Cancer Database, leading to a deep understanding of familial relative risks (Sud et al., 2019; Kharazmi et al., 2012; Hemminki and Czene, 2002).
evidence: Explicit statement with citations to support the claim.

claim: The Victorian Paediatric Cancer Family Study in Australia explored the cancer risks for relatives of children with cancer in a small population.
source: The Victorian Paediatric Cancer Family Study in Australia also explored the cancer risks for relatives of children with cancer in a small population (Heath et al., 2014).
evidence: Explicit statement with citation to support the claim.

claim: The Utah Population database is one of the best-known populations for studying familial risk in the United States.
source: In the United States, the Utah Population database may be the best-known population for studying familial risk (Curtin et al., 2013; Kohli et al., 2019; Samadder et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2010; Goldgar et al., 1994).
evidence: Explicit statement with multiple citations to support the claim.

claim: Previous familial risk studies largely comprise families of European ancestry and have not examined potential ethnic-specific familial risks.
source: Importantly, these studies largely comprise families of European ancestry, and therefore have not examined potential ethnic-specific familial risks.
evidence: Direct statement about the limitation of previous studies.

claim: This is the first study to quantify the familial clustering risks and risks of SPMs among early-onset cancer patients with an emphasis on racial/ethnic differences.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first study to quantify the familial clustering risks and risks of SPMs among early-onset cancer patients with an emphasis on racial/ethnic differences.
evidence: Direct statement claiming novelty of the study.

claim: The information on fathers was not available until 2004 in the birth files and therefore is not included in the current analysis.
source: The information on healthy siblings and mothers was available during the whole study period, whereas the information on fathers was not available until 2004 in the birth files and therefore is not included in the current analysis.
evidence: Direct statement about data availability limitations.

claim: A physician reviewed diagnosis codes of all the cases diagnosed after the first primary case to prevent the misclassification of relapsed first primary malignancies (FPMs) as SPMs.
source: A physician (EN) reviewed diagnosis codes of all the cases diagnosed after the first primary case to prevent the misclassification of relapsed first primary malignancies (FPMs) as SPMs.
evidence: Direct statement about the quality control procedure.

claim: Cancers were classified into 12 broad groups and subgroups as defined by the International Classification of Childhood Cancer, Third edition (ICCC-3, November 2012).
source: For both analyses, we classified the cancers into 12 broad groups and subgroups as defined by the International Classification of Childhood Cancer, Third edition (ICCC-3, November 2012) (https://seer.cancer.gov/iccc/iccc3.html).
evidence: Direct statement about the classification system used.

claim: Hematologic cancers were defined as leukemias and lymphomas.
source: Hematologic cancers were defined as leukemias and lymphomas.
evidence: Direct definition statement.

claim: Solid cancers were defined as central nervous system (CNS) tumors, neuroblastomas, retinoblastomas, renal tumors, hepatic tumors, bone tumors, sarcomas, germ cell tumors, epithelial neoplasms, and other and unspecified malignant neoplasms.
source: Solid cancers were defined as central nervous system (CNS) tumors, neuroblastomas, retinoblastomas, renal tumors, hepatic tumors, bone tumors, sarcomas, germ cell tumors, epithelial neoplasms, and other and unspecified malignant neoplasms.
evidence: Direct definition statement.

claim: A proband was defined as a pediatric or AYA patient with a given cancer, with only one child/AYA in each family being a proband.
source: We defined a proband as a pediatric or AYA patient with a given cancer. Only one child/AYA in each family can be a proband, so that in families with two or more cases, the proband is defined as the patient with the earliest date of diagnosis.
evidence: Direct definition statement.

claim: In families with two or more cases, the proband is defined as the patient with the earliest date of diagnosis.
source: Only one child/AYA in each family can be a proband, so that in families with two or more cases, the proband is defined as the patient with the earliest date of diagnosis.
evidence: Direct definition statement.

claim: The analyses were stratified by self-identified race/ethnicity of the mother in each family.
source: Separately, we calculated the SIRs for a sibling for the same type of cancer as the proband. We also stratified the analyses by self-identified race/ethnicity of the mother in each family.
evidence: Direct statement about the stratification approach.

claim: For siblings and mothers, age was stratified into seven groups as 0, 0–4, 5–9, 10–14, 15–19, 20–24, and 25–29 years.
source: For siblings and mothers, age was stratified into seven groups as 0, 0–4, 5–9, 10–14, 15–19, 20–24, and 25–29 years.
evidence: Direct statement about the age stratification method.

claim: The 95% CIs were calculated assuming a Poisson distribution for categories with less than 100 observed cases.
source: The 95% CIs were calculated assuming a Poisson distribution for categories with less than 100 observed cases.
evidence: Direct statement about the statistical method used.

claim: For categories with more than 100 observed cases, the method indicated by Breslow and Day, 1987 was adopted to calculate the 95% CIs.
source: For categories with more than 100 observed cases, we adopted the method as indicated by Breslow and Day, 1987 to calculate the 95% CIs, as suggested by Washington State Department of Health (Guidelines for Using Confidence Intervals for Public Health Assessment, 2012; Breslow and Day, 1987).
evidence: Direct statement about the statistical method used with citations.

claim: Statistical analyses were performed using R software (v 3.6.0).
source: Statistical analyses were performed using R software (v 3.6.0).
evidence: Direct statement about the software used.

claim: Any two-sided p-value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
source: Any two-sided p-value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
evidence: Direct statement about the significance threshold.

claim: Increased relative risks of any cancer for siblings and mothers were observed given a proband with lymphoid leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia, Hodgkin lymphomas, non-Hodgkin lymphomas, astrocytomas, intracranial and intraspinal embryonal tumors, certain gliomas, certain specified intracranial and intraspinal neoplasms, nephroblastoma and other nonepithelial renal tumors, rhabdomyosarcomas, fibrosarcomas, peripheral nerve sheath tumors and other fibrous neoplasms, certain specified soft tissue sarcomas, malignant gonadal germ cell tumors, and certain unspecified carcinomas.
source: When stratified by more finely defined cancer subtypes, increased relative risks of any cancer for siblings and mothers were observed given a proband with lymphoid leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia, Hodgkin lymphomas, non-Hodgkin lymphomas, astrocytomas, intracranial and intraspinal embryonal tumors, certain gliomas, certain specified intracranial and intraspinal neoplasms, nephroblastoma and other nonepithelial renal tumors, rhabdomyosarcomas, fibrosarcomas, peripheral nerve sheath tumors and other fibrous neoplasms, certain specified soft tissue sarcomas, malignant gonadal germ cell tumors, and certain unspecified carcinomas (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: Explicit statement about findings for specific cancer subtypes.

claim: The findings of elevated familial risk were consistent across race/ethnic groups, but the magnitude was different.
source: The findings were consistent across race/ethnic groups; however, the magnitude was different.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing the pattern of findings.

claim: Latinos and non-Latino Blacks had higher sibling/maternal relative risks compared to NLWs for solid cancers.
source: Latinos and non-Latino Blacks had higher sibling/maternal relative risks compared to NLWs for solid cancers, and APIs exhibited a higher risk of hematologic neoplasms.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing the ethnic differences.

claim: APIs exhibited a higher risk of hematologic neoplasms compared to NLWs.
source: Latinos and non-Latino Blacks had higher sibling/maternal relative risks compared to NLWs for solid cancers, and APIs exhibited a higher risk of hematologic neoplasms.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing the ethnic differences.

claim: A rich literature with a primary focus on European ancestry populations has reported excessive familial risks of hematologic malignancies.
source: Consistent with our results, a rich literature with a primary focus on European ancestry populations has reported excessive familial risks of hematologic malignancies (Sud et al., 2019), lymphomas (Cerhan and Slager, 2015; Fallah et al., 2016; Madanat‐Harjuoja et al., 2020), brain tumors (Couldwell and Cannon-Albright, 2017; Crump et al., 2015), neuroblastomas (Kamihara et al., 2017), retinoblastomas (Madanat‐Harjuoja et al., 2020; Kamihara et al., 2017), germ cell tumors (Landero-Huerta et al., 2017), sarcomas (Lynch et al., 2003), and melanomas (Frank et al., 2017).
evidence: Explicit statement with citation to support the claim.

claim: Studies have reported excessive risks of SPMs among survivors of hereditary retinoblastoma.
source: In terms of secondary cancers, studies have reported excessive risks of SPMs among of survivors of hereditary retinoblastoma (Marees et al., 2008), chronic myeloid leukemia (Sasaki et al., 2019), chronic lymphocytic leukemia (Molica, 2005), Hodgkin's lymphoma (Baker, 2016), non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (Chattopadhyay et al., 2018), and neuroblastoma (Applebaum et al., 2015).
evidence: Explicit statement with citation to support the claim.

claim: The excessive familial risks of certain cancers are highly likely to be associated with genetic predisposition.
source: The excessive familial risks of certain cancers are highly likely to be associated with genetic predisposition.
evidence: Direct statement expressing a strong inference about causation.

claim: Germline loss-of-function mutations in RB1 are found in ~40% of retinoblastoma cases.
source: The archetypic examples are germline loss-of-function mutations in RB1, which are found in ~40% of retinoblastoma cases (Kamihara et al., 2017), and adrenal cortical cancer, with germline TP53 mutations accounting for most familial cases (Kamihara et al., 2017).
evidence: Explicit statement with citation to support the claim.

claim: Germline TP53 mutations account for most familial cases of adrenal cortical cancer.
source: The archetypic examples are germline loss-of-function mutations in RB1, which are found in ~40% of retinoblastoma cases (Kamihara et al., 2017), and adrenal cortical cancer, with germline TP53 mutations accounting for most familial cases (Kamihara et al., 2017).
evidence: Explicit statement with citation to support the claim.

claim: Combinations of low-frequency alleles or 'polygenic risk scores' have been shown to be as impactful as single strong predisposition mutations in adult cancers.
source: Low penetrance common genetic variations, for instance in CEBPE, IKZF1, and ARID5B genes in ALL, are associated with cancer risk and may also contribute to familial concordance as combinations of low-frequency alleles or 'polygenic risk scores' have been shown to be as impactful as single strong predisposition mutations in adult cancers (Fantus and Helfand, 2019; Yadav and Couch, 2019); however, their contribution to cancer clustering among children and their families has not yet been studied.
evidence: Explicit statement with citations to support the claim.

claim: The contribution of polygenic risk scores to cancer clustering among children and their families has not yet been studied.
source: Low penetrance common genetic variations, for instance in CEBPE, IKZF1, and ARID5B genes in ALL, are associated with cancer risk and may also contribute to familial concordance as combinations of low-frequency alleles or 'polygenic risk scores' have been shown to be as impactful as single strong predisposition mutations in adult cancers (Fantus and Helfand, 2019; Yadav and Couch, 2019); however, their contribution to cancer clustering among children and their families has not yet been studied.
evidence: Direct statement about a research gap.
